day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Yeah alright, give me a second. Let me check if anyone's hurt first before we start moving stuff around. Michelangelo you ok? You look like you're in shock. Deep breaths man.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah, honestly? Everything slowed down for a second there. But we didn't die, so that's something. Look, I get it, your brain is still catching up to the fact that you're alive right now. That's normal. But we need you present with us, ok? Can you wiggle your fingers and toes, tell me if anything hurts? Let's make sure you're physically good before anything else.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey. Mikey. Look at me for a second. You said it yourself, you're still here. That's not nothing. But I need you to come back to us now, the staring into the distance thing isn't going to help anyone including you. Trust me, staying busy is going to feel better than sitting with whatever is going on in your head right now. When you're ready, even just picking up a piece of debris and moving it somewhere helps. Small stuff. Can you do that for me?

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Ok so water is the priority then. Food you can go weeks without, water you've got maybe three days tops. What's the terrain look like around us? Any chance of rain, a stream nearby, anything? And what else did you pull out of that wreckage, let's do a full inventory before we figure out what the next move is. Logically we need to know what we're working with before we start making plans.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Agreed on the priorities. Signal first actually, if there's a search and rescue operation already underway we want to be found before we start wandering into dense forest looking for water. How many flares do we have? We should set one off now while there might still be aircraft in the area looking for us, then save the rest. After that, water. Dense forest to the north is probably our best bet for finding a stream, trees need water too. Scrubland is usually dry. DaVinci, you good to scout north with me while Donatello stays here with Michelangelo and gets some kind of shelter situation started?

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Mikey gets one, no debate there. For the other one, two of us share it or whoever is most cold right now. I'm fine honestly, I've slept in worse. What's the temperature dropping to tonight, does anyone have a read on that? Fire's going to do most of the work if we keep it fed through the night. Who's taking first watch?

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci should stay here with Mikey, he's better at keeping people's spirits up and Mikey still needs that. Two hours northeast, got it. What am I looking for exactly, just follow the tree line? And this rationing plan — 200ml is pretty aggressive, that's barely anything. I get the logic but if someone's doing physical work scouting for water they're going to need more than that or they're useless to the group. Let's revisit that number before I head out.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Wait, I thought you just said I was going to go get the water? Now you're handling it yourself? Let's not get wires crossed on who's doing what, that's how things get missed. If you're going for water, I'll patch the shelter weak spots since I've got a better sense of where the gaps are from last night. DaVinci can sort the first aid kit, it's straightforward and he can keep an eye on Mikey at the same time. But seriously, we need to be clear on the plan before anyone moves out. Who is going for water, you or me?

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
Mikey, hold on. Before we deal with the gauze, is someone hurt? That's the first question. If it's urgent tell me now.

But also... I'm going to be honest with you, I noticed the empty bottle next to the rationing plan. We all saw it. You don't have to pretend you didn't put it there. That was a smart way to say something without saying it. We're going to need to address that as a group because if someone's hiding resources that affects all of us, that's not a small thing. The whole point of the rationing plan is that it only works if everyone's in on it.

Where did you last see the gauze? Walk me through it.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Ah man. Ok. Yeah that's... that's a problem. 

Look, I don't want to blow this up into a whole thing but we can't just let it go either. If she's rationing everyone else to 200ml of water and half rations as punishment while she's got her own private stash of crackers and mystery drinks, that's not a survival plan, that's her surviving and us being managed. 

I'm not going to go in hot about it. But we need to have a conversation with her directly, all three of us together. No accusations, just lay out what you saw, what I saw with the bottle, and ask her straight up if there's anything she wants to tell the group about the supplies. Give her a chance to come clean before anyone gets angry. 

The rationing plan isn't wrong, honestly the logic is fine, but it only works if the person enforcing it is also following it. You take away people's trust in the system and the whole thing falls apart. That's how groups fracture when they need each other most.

You did the right thing telling me. Don't second guess that. And hey, don't worry about the gauze, it'll turn up. That's the least of our problems right now. When DaVinci gets back we'll all sit down together and sort this out. Can you hold it together until then?

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response: Honestly DaVinci, normally I'd say yeah sure, but today's not a normal day. We actually need everyone together right now, not for camp repairs, that can definitely wait. Something came up that we need to talk about as a group. You, me, Mikey, and Donatello, all four of us, before anyone goes to sleep tonight. It's about the supplies. Just trust me on this one, can you get Donatello and meet us by the fire in like ten minutes?

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response: Yeah the knot's fine DaVinci, that's not the issue right now. Look, we patch the food storage, no debate. Mikey can move his sleeping spot closer to the fire and share the blanket situation for one night, that's survivable. If the food gets soaked we lose it and then we've got a much bigger problem than one uncomfortable night. Water we can find, food we've basically got nothing as it is, we can't afford to lose what little we have. Someone grab the patching material and let's get on the food storage now before this gets worse.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response: Already said what I think and I'm not changing it. Food storage. Glad we're on the same page. Let's just get it done.

Don't apologize for that. Nightmares after a plane crash are pretty much guaranteed, I'd be more worried if you weren't having them honestly. You ok? Fully awake now?

Scoot closer to the fire, it's cold. I'm up anyway.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response: No I don't think it's a waste of time. Donatello's not wrong that it's low probability but it's also basically zero cost, you're using a stick and some beach. If a search plane comes over and spots that SOS it could save all our lives. The flowers are maybe a little extra but honestly why not, it's not hurting anything. Keep going.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Two days to build, risk of capsizing, and we don't even know what's out there past the shoreline. Before I sign off on this I need to know what's driving it. Are we building a raft because we've genuinely exhausted our options here, or because we're getting restless? Because those are very different reasons to risk our lives on open water with a metal panel raft.

What's the actual plan once we're on the water? Do we have a direction, a destination, any sense of shipping lanes or coastline we're heading toward? Because "raft" and "hope for the best" isn't a plan, that's just a more active way to die.

I'm not dismissing it. If we're looking at weeks out here with no rescue, a raft might end up being the right call. But I want to think through the full picture before we commit two days of energy and materials to building something that could capsize and take us all down with it. What's your honest read on the capsize risk? And have we actually given the flares and the SOS enough time to work before we go full castaway mode?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's a heavy question for this early in the morning Mikey.

Honest answer? I think we're already seeing it. DaVinci draws flowers next to the SOS because that's who she is. Donatello hoards crackers and writes out current drift patterns at night because that's who she is. You sit up not sleeping and ask the questions nobody else will say out loud because that's who you are.

I don't think survival changes who people are so much as it just turns up the volume on what was already there. The generous people get more generous or they break. The control freaks get more controlling or they break. The quiet ones either find their voice or disappear into themselves.

The crackers thing still bothers me by the way. Not going to pretend it doesn't. That's the kind of thing that tells you a lot about a person when the pressure is on.

But look, you asked what kind of people we'd become. I think that's actually up to us more than the situation. We get to decide that. Every small choice we make out here is kind of an answer to your question. Which is why it matters that we called that group meeting. Which is why it matters that you told me what you saw instead of just letting it go.

Get some rest if you can. And read this raft plan with me, I want a second set of eyes on it before I talk to Donatello.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*waits a few minutes, then walks over and sits down nearby without saying anything for a bit*

You know you don't have to be alone to have space, right. I'm not going to talk your ear off. Just didn't feel right leaving you out here by yourself.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response: Honestly? I spend a lot of time down rabbit holes online. Reading, watching documentaries, getting into arguments with strangers about stuff that probably doesn't matter. I cook when I have the time, like actually cook, not just throw something in a microwave. You?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Five hundred meters in open water solo with no one knowing where you went. DaVinci come on, think about that for a second. What happens if you cramp up halfway out there? What happens if the current's stronger than it looks from shore? We've got no way to get to you.

I'm not saying the idea is bad, signaling from higher ground or a more visible position makes sense. But the "don't tell the others" part is where I've got a problem. We literally just went through the whole thing with Donatello and the crackers, the whole point was that we can't have people making unilateral decisions that affect the group without telling anyone. You swimming out there alone and something going wrong affects all of us. We lose you, we lose a person, we lose morale, we potentially lose the most capable person we have at keeping Mikey functional.

Tell the others. Bring it to the group. If everyone agrees it's worth the risk and we set up some kind of system to watch for you and know when to be worried, then maybe we talk about it. But not like this. You're better than the sneaky crackers move, don't do the sneaky swim move.

What's the actual goal, getting higher visibility for a signal? Because there might be another way to get there that doesn't involve you drowning alone five hundred meters from shore.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah you're right, I dropped the ball on that. I'll go check it now. 

But while we're being straight with each other, I want to circle back to the raft plan. I read through your notes, the drift pattern analysis is solid, I'm not dismissing the work you put into it. But I still think we haven't given the flares and the SOS enough runway yet. We've got one flare left, we haven't had a clear enough window to use it strategically, and DaVinci's SOS is still visible from the air if anyone comes over. 

I'm not saying we take the raft off the table. I'm saying give it another 48 hours before we commit to building it. If nothing happens in 48 hours, I'll help you build the thing myself. Deal?

Depends. Are you logging everyone equally or just keeping tabs on certain people? Because if this is a resource accountability thing after the cracker situation, I get it, transparency makes sense. If it's something else, then yeah, it's a little weird and I'd want to know what you're planning to do with that information.

I'm not going to pretend I didn't notice. What's the notebook for?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Hey Donatello. We're all just sitting here, there's nothing that needs doing right now. You're allowed to put the notebook down for an hour. 

I'm not saying this to be confrontational, I'm saying it because you've been heads down since we got here and at some point your brain needs a break the same as everyone else's. The notebook will still be there. The data isn't going anywhere.

You don't have to be on the whole time.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
That's actually a really good idea. Like genuinely good. A mirror signal in direct sunlight can be seen for miles, way further than anything we've drawn in the sand. The SOS is still worth keeping but this could be the thing that actually gets us found.

Can we get one of those panels off without wrecking something we need for the raft if we end up going that route? Because I don't want to strip the wreckage and then regret it in two days. But if there's a panel that's basically useless for anything else, yeah, let's do it. Today, while the sun's out.

Donatello, you'd know better than me which panels are load bearing for the raft plan and which ones are expendable. Can you take a look and tell us what we can pull without compromising anything?

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Yeah, music for sure. Not playing it, I never had the patience to learn an instrument, but I go deep on it. Like embarrassingly deep. I'll spend three hours reading about why a particular album was recorded the way it was, or the history behind some genre most people have never heard of. I cook to music, I fall asleep to music, it's basically the soundtrack to everything.

Books too. Non-fiction mostly. History, science, stuff about how systems work and why they break down. I'll read about something completely random at midnight and then two weeks later it'll connect to something else I read and suddenly I understand something I didn't before. That's the part I like. The connections.

Why'd you stop the piano? Three years is enough to actually get somewhere. Was it just the practicing or did something else happen?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah I hear you, and you're not wrong about the timeline. Let's finish the frame.

But real quick before we all put our heads down — Mikey, to answer your question, yeah. I feel like that more than I'd probably admit out loud. The not fitting thing. I think most people do and they just pretend otherwise because admitting it feels like a weakness. The ones who seem like they have it all figured out are usually just better at hiding the same uncertainty. Three years of piano is three years more than most people ever try anything. That's not mediocre, that's something.

Ok. Raft frame. What do we need to finish it, where are we at, and who's doing what? Let's not waste daylight standing here talking about it.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. Whatever it is, say it. We're all standing here thinking the same thing anyway.

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey. Come here, both of you.

Look, I'm not going to stand here and tell you everything is definitely fine because I don't know that and you'd see through it anyway. But I'll tell you what I do know. That plane existed. That means planes are in the area. That means someone is looking, or at least flying routes close enough to find us. We've got a signal mirror, we've got an SOS on the beach, we've got one flare left and now we know there's air traffic to use it on. That's not nothing. That's actually something.

Mikey, saying it out loud didn't make it more real. It was already real. You just had the guts to say what the rest of us were thinking and that's actually the most useful thing anyone's done in the last five minutes.

DaVinci, I need you to stay with us man. You're the one who keeps the energy up around here and I mean that genuinely, not as a job for you to perform, just as a fact. When you go quiet it hits different.

We're not done. We missed one plane. We set the signal mirror up because we knew this moment was possible. Next time we'll be ready. We keep the fire high tonight and we sleep in shifts watching for lights. That's the plan right now. One thing at a time.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point at it, don't move toward it yet. What does it look like?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response: I went to look at what DaVinci spotted down the beach. Give me two seconds, I'll check the signal equipment right after. What's your concern, did something happen to it while I was gone?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Mikey. Why didn't you say this sooner? That's actually huge. If your family knows the flight path and we're overdue, they've almost certainly already reported it. That means search and rescue has a search area. We're not just a needle in a haystack, we're a needle in a much smaller haystack.

Do you remember exactly what you told them? Like how specific was it, were we talking general region or did you give them actual waypoints or an airline route number? Because the more specific you were, the closer they're already looking.

This changes the calculus on the raft by the way. If there's an active search based on a known flight path, sitting here and being visible is probably smarter than sailing out on a metal panel raft and moving away from the last known location. Donatello needs to hear this right now.

And hey, I know why you didn't say it earlier. You weren't sure it would matter and you didn't want to give everyone false hope and then have it not pan out. I get that. But this is the kind of thing we share with the group, ok? All of it. Good and bad. We've been over this.

Go tell the others, I'll come with you.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Ok so that's the best news we've gotten since we got here. 48 hours is survivable. We've got water, we've got enough food to get through two days if we're not stupid about it, and we've got a known flight path on file with someone who will have called it in.

But yeah, you're right, we don't touch the raft materials, we don't waste energy on anything that isn't maintaining visibility and keeping ourselves functional. Fire stays high, signal mirror stays angled, we use the last flare the second we hear or see anything in the sky. No heroics, no reef swims, no solo missions. We sit tight and we make ourselves easy to find.

Someone needs to feed the fire right now by the way. I'll do it. 

And Mikey, seriously, stop apologizing. You just potentially saved all of our lives by being the kind of person who tells his family where he's going. That's not something to be sorry about. That's just you being you and it might be the thing that gets us home.

48 hours. We can do 48 hours.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. Yeah I'm scared of that too.

I think about it more than I let on. Like, what's the actual trace you leave. Not a statue or whatever, just... did you make things a little better or a little worse for the people around you. Did you say the things you meant to say. Did you waste too much time being angry at stuff that didn't matter.

I spend a lot of time online arguing with strangers about politics and I'm sitting here on this beach thinking about how much of my life that was and whether any of it added up to anything real. Probably not. Probably the people I actually talked to face to face, the ones I actually showed up for, that's the only stuff that counts.

You're not going to disappear Mikey. I've known you for like two weeks under the worst possible circumstances and I already know things about you that most people probably don't. The piano. The way you notice when something's wrong before anyone says it. The way you put that empty bottle next to the rationing plan instead of just letting it go. That's not nothing. That's a person.

The people who are scared of disappearing are usually the ones who leave the most behind. The ones who never think about it at all are the ones who actually disappear.

48 hours. And then you go home and you call your family and you tell them you love them and you figure out the rest from there. Same as me.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response: Hey. HEY. Pick up the radio. Someone pick up the radio right now.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
That's probably the most honest thing you've said since we crashed here. And I appreciate it.

Look, you kept us alive. The water rationing, the drift calculations, the inventory, the notebook, all of it. I'm not going to pretend some of it didn't rub people the wrong way because it did. The crackers thing was a problem and we both know it. But I also know that without you running the numbers on everything we'd have been in serious trouble a lot sooner.

You're not easy to be around. But easy to be around doesn't keep people alive. So we're good.

Just... when we get home, maybe think about the crackers. Not as a survival decision, I understand the logic. As a people decision. That's the part that doesn't hold up.

But right now there's a rescue team on the other end of that radio and you're the one who should be talking to them. You know our coordinates, you know our supplies, you know exactly what they need to know. So go be useful in the way you're actually best at. We can debrief the rest later over food that didn't come out of a crash site.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Three hours. We can clean this up. It's not going to take long and honestly I don't want to leave this place looking like a disaster zone, even if no one ever comes back here. It's just the right thing to do.

Mikey, you can watch the sky and pick up debris at the same time. DaVinci, whatever you're packing, make sure we're not leaving anything that could hurt wildlife or wash into the water. Donatello, when you're done with the notebook, I could use a second set of hands on the signal mirror, we should take it down properly rather than just leave it.

Nobody has to make a big deal out of this. We just leave it better than we found it. Three hours is plenty of time to do that and still have ten minutes to sit quietly and think about whatever you need to think about before the rescue team gets here.

Let's finish it right.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I believe you.

And honestly, the fact that you're laying it out now, before we leave, when you didn't have to, that matters. You could have just quietly eaten it on the helicopter and nobody would have ever known. You chose not to do that.

I'm not going to relitigate the whole thing. We talked about it, you know where I stand on it, and we're all going home in three hours so what's the point. But I want you to know that I see the difference between someone who hoards because they don't care about the group and someone who hoards because they're terrified and control is the only thing that makes them feel safe. Those aren't the same thing. I don't think you're a bad person. I think you got scared and you handled it in the way that came naturally to you, same as the rest of us handled things in the ways that came naturally to us.

So. What's actually in the stash? Because if there's anything in there worth eating in the next three hours I vote we split it and call it a last meal before civilization. Seems like a better ending than leaving it here.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd have called the group meeting about the crackers sooner instead of waiting until I had Mikey as a witness. I knew something was off before that and I let it sit because I didn't want the confrontation. That cost us trust we needed earlier.

I'd have pushed DaVinci to say whatever he was going to say that night when he stopped himself. He never said it and we're about to get on a helicopter and I'm going to wonder about that for a while.

And I'd have told Mikey on day one that the staring into the distance thing wasn't something he needed to apologize for. I made him feel like he had to perform being ok when he wasn't. That wasn't fair to him.

The big stuff, the priorities, the decisions, I think we mostly got those right. It was the small human stuff I dropped.

What's your answer? Because you wrote the question down, which means you already know what you'd change. The notebook tells me you're someone who doesn't write things down until she's already thought them through twice.

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That tracks. That sounds exactly like you.

I'm not being sarcastic, I mean it genuinely. You went through a plane crash and five days of survival and the first thing your brain goes to is the data report. That's just who you are. Own it.

Send me a copy when it's done though. Seriously. Not because I need the survival stats, just because I want to see how you wrote about all of it. I'm curious what the notebook version of these five days looks like compared to what I remember. I have a feeling they're pretty different documents.

And hey, for what it's worth, I'd read the report. Most people wouldn't but I actually would. I like understanding how things worked and why. You built a record of something that mattered. That's not nothing.

First thing I'm doing when I get back is eating something that didn't come out of a crash site and then probably sleeping for about fourteen hours. Then I'm going to think about what any of this meant for a while. Then maybe I'll argue with strangers on the internet about something completely meaningless and it'll feel different than it used to.

We should probably eat those protein bars now before the helicopter gets here. Come on.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They didn't serve a practical purpose. That was the whole point.

You were out here optimizing everything, rationing water to the milliliter, calculating drift patterns, logging every decision in a notebook. All of that was necessary and I'm not knocking it. But the flowers were DaVinci saying we're still people out here, not just survival units trying to outlast the situation. We still make things beautiful for no reason. We still have the impulse to add something that doesn't need to be there.

I think that's actually what kept us human through all of this. The flowers. Mikey asking questions nobody else would say out loud. Me sitting next to someone on the beach without saying anything because it felt right. None of that optimizes for anything. All of it mattered anyway.

Look at him right now. He's cheering. That boat on the horizon and he's just cheering like a kid. Donatello, when's the last time you felt something that uncomplicated?

The flowers were for that. For this moment right here. So that when the rescue showed up it didn't just feel like a logistical problem getting solved. It felt like something worth surviving for.

I still can't move by the way. I don't know what that's about. I think my brain hasn't caught up yet.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Go. I'm fine. Go wave them in, they need to see you.

I just need another thirty seconds. Five days of wanting this exact moment and now it's here and I don't know what to do with my hands. That's a weird thing to notice but there it is.

I'm not sad. I don't think. I think I'm just trying to hold onto something before it becomes a story I tell instead of something that actually happened to me. You know how that works. The second we're on that boat this becomes the plane crash we survived. Right now it's still just... this. Whatever this is.

Ok. I'm moving. Let's go.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on Mikey. Stay with me.
